'''Peter Neil Temple Wells''' (19 May 1936 in [[Bristol]], England – 22 April 2017)<ref>[http://www.cardiff.ac.uk/news/view/734859-professor-peter-wells-cbe-1936-2017 Professor Peter Wells CBE (1936 – 2017)]</ref> was a British [[medical physics|medical physicist]] who played a major role in the application of [[ultrasound]] technology in medicine.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.ob-ultrasound.net/pwells.html|title=Wells Biography at obstetric ultrasound website|website=ob-ultrasound.net}}</ref><ref name=whoswho/><ref>[https://www.pressreader.com/uk/the-daily-telegraph/20170711/282312500107595 Professor Peter Wells]</ref>

==Education==
Wells was educated at [[Aston University|Birmingham College of Advanced Technology]]<ref name=whoswho>{{Who's Who | title=WELLS, Prof. Peter Neil Temple | id = U4000364 | volume = 2004 | edition = online [[Oxford University Press]]|location=Oxford}}</ref> and the [[University of Bristol]] where he was awarded his [[PhD]] in 1966.<ref name=whoswho/>

==Career and research==
Wells made a number of notable contributions to the application of engineering and physics in medicine – he was the originator and developer of instruments for ultrasonic surgery and ultrasonic power measurement, as well as the two-dimensional, articulated-arm ultrasonic general purpose scanner and the water-immersion [[Mammography|ultrasonic breast scanner]].<ref name=frs/>

He demonstrated ultrasonic-pulsed Doppler range gating, and was the discoverer of the ultrasonic Doppler signal characteristic of malignant tumour [[neovascularisation]]. He investigated ultrasonic bioeffects and formulated ultrasonic safety guidelines and conditions for prudent use of ultrasonic diagnosis.<ref name=frs/>

Wells led multidisciplinary studies of ultrasonic diagnosis and made major contributions to the advancement of light transmission, electrical impedance and nuclear magnetic resonance imaging, as well as to interventional telepresence. He also proposed a novel philosophy of medical imaging. In the early part of the 21st century, he was developing ultrasonic [[Doppler effect|Doppler]] and phase-insensitive [[tomography]].<ref name=frs/>
